q-49545.name: Question 1
q-49545.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/16)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/16}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

  

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(x/4)}^{2}}}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-2506.name: Question 2
q-2506.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $9{x}^{2}=(3x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-9{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(3x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-114022.name: Question 3
q-114022.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{\sqrt{1-25{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =5\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(5x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/9)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/9}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.

$$

q-114040.name: Question 6
q-114040.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $2{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{2}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{1+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{1+(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

q-114046.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{9}{81\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/81)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/81}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

 The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{9})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{9}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{9}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=9\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{81+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/9)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (9\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{9})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|\sqrt{2}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{2}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{2}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|\sqrt{2}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{2}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Calculate ∫1|x|2x2−1dx.

a
2arcsec(2x)+C
b
2arcsec(x)+C
c
arcsec(x2)+C
d
2arcsec(2x)+C
e
arcsec(2x)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that we can rewrite this integral as ∫dx|x|2x2−1=∫2|2x|(2x)2−1dx.

This integral now resembles the basic one for arcsec, ∫1|u|u2−1du=arcsec(u)+C.

The only difference is that instead of u as the variable, we have 2x.

So, let's substitute u=2x. Differentiating, we get dudx=2⟹dx=12du.

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of u and evaluate: ∫1|x|2x2−1dx=∫2|2x|(2x)2−1dx=2∫1|u|u2−1⋅(12du)=2⋅12∫du|u|u2−1=arcsec u+C=arcsec(2x)+C

q-114055.name: Question 12
q-114055.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{7}{|x|\sqrt{7{x}^{2}-1}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{7\sqrt{7}}{|\sqrt{7}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{7}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{7}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{7}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{|x|\sqrt{7{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{7\sqrt{7}}{|\sqrt{7}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{7}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =7\sqrt{7}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\text{d}u) \\  & =7\sqrt{7}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =7\,\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =7\,\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{7}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-73716.name: Question 13
q-73716.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $4x.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|4x|\sqrt{(4x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(4x)}{4}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{|\sqrt{5}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{5}x.$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{|\sqrt{5}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{5}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{5}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

The only difference is that instead of u as the variable, we have 5x.

q-114057.name: Question 15
q-114057.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{100{x}^{2}-1}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{50}{|10x|\sqrt{(10x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $10x.$

So, let's substitute $u=10x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{10}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{|x|\sqrt{100{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{50}{|10x|\sqrt{(10x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =50\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{10}\text{d}u) \\  & =50\cdot \frac{1}{10}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =5\,\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =5\,\text{arcsec}(10x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
